Here are the verse-by-verse notes on **1 Chronicles 28**, drawn from the available pages (search/fetch limits were reached, so some traditions and modern‑critical sources could not be fully retrieved; gaps are noted).

---

## Overview of the Chapter

**David’s public “passing of the torch”** — an aged King David summons the leaders of Israel, publicly designates Solomon as his successor, delivers the Divinely‑revealed temple plans, and charges both the people and Solomon to be faithful. The Chronicler presents David as a second Moses and Solomon as a second Joshua (Payne, cited by Constable and Enduring Word).

---

## Verse‑by‑Verse Notes

### v. 1 — The Great Assembly Gathered
David summoned to Jerusalem every category of leader: tribal princes, military commanders (thousands and hundreds), stewards of royal property and livestock, court officials, and all the mighty men of valor.

- **Gill** notes that the persons listed correspond to the officers enumerated in 1 Chronicles 27: the tribal princes (27:16–22), the captains of the monthly divisions (27:2), captains of thousands and hundreds, stewards (27:25–31), and the mighty men (11:10–47). He calls this “David’s public passing‑of‑the‑torch ceremony.”
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/28.htm
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)** notes that this assembly was the formal “passing of the torch” with emphasis on the responsibility to build the temple, and observes that despite this, another son (Adonijah, 1 Kings 1–2) tried to seize the throne. The verse repeats the assembly of 1 Chronicles 23:2 — a literary device to resume the narrative after the intervening material of chapters 23–27 (Thompson, cited by Precept Austin).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-28/
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-28-commentary
- **Utley** (cited at Precept Austin) observes that surprisingly the priests and Levites are not emphasized here, unlike elsewhere in Chronicles.
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-28-commentary

### v. 2 — David Rises to Speak: His Heart’s Desire
Despite his frailty (1 Kings 1:1–4), David rose to his feet and addressed the assembly as “my brothers and my people.” He declares it was in his heart to build a “house of rest” for the ark and a “footstool for our God,” and that he had made preparations.

- **Gill** says David rose from his bed or couch, having been stricken with a paralytic disorder; standing was an act of exertion and honor. He notes David’s humility in calling his subjects “my brethren” — a type of Christ (cf. Heb. 2:11).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/28.htm
- **Gaebelein** writes that David’s three postures are suggestive: on his face as a penitent, sitting before the Lord as a worshipper (1 Chr 17:16), and now standing as a servant.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-chronicles-28.html
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**, citing Selman, notes why David calls the temple a “house of rest”: just as God’s Sabbath rest at creation meant completion of His work, so the temple would be the place of God’s settled presence. David as a “man of war” could only prepare the conditions; only Solomon the “man of rest” (1 Chr 22:9) could build.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-28/
- **Precept Austin** adds that “footstool” (*hadom*) is a royal symbol — the ark as the place where heaven and earth meet, the visible expression of the invisible God’s sovereign rule.
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-28-commentary

### v. 3 — God’s “No” to David
God told David he could not build the house for God’s Name because he was a man of war who had shed blood.

- **Gill** references 2 Samuel 7:5 (Nathan’s message) and 1 Chronicles 22:8 as parallel passages.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/28.htm
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)** notes God “politely refused” David’s offer and instead proposed to build David a “house” (a lasting dynasty).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-28/
- **Precept Austin** offers a pastoral application from Alan Redpath: many believers have had ambitions to do great things for God — to be missionaries, preachers, leaders — but God has said “no” through sickness, different callings, or closed doors. The question is how we respond to a frustrated ambition that God has cut across.
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-28-commentary

### v. 4 — God’s Election of David
The LORD chose David out of all his father’s house to be king. God chose Judah as the ruling tribe, then the house of Jesse, and among Jesse’s sons He was pleased with David.

- **Gill** traces the steps: God chose Judah (1 Chr 5:2; Gen 49:8), then Jesse’s family (1 Sam 16:1), then David, the youngest (1 Sam 16:10–11). “Over Israel forever” means for a long duration in his posterity, and ultimately fulfilled in Christ (Luke 1:32).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/28.htm
- **The Pulpit Commentary** (retrieved via search excerpt) notes the same four‑step election: tribe, house, father, self — echoing 1 Samuel 16:1–13.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-28.html
- **Constable** observes that the Chronicler is highlighting the Davidic Covenant as the heartbeat of the book, pointing toward a faithful Son of David yet to come.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-28.html

### v. 5 — Solomon Chosen from Among Many Sons
God chose Solomon — out of all David’s many sons — to sit on “the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel.”

- **Gill** lists David’s sons born in Hebron and Jerusalem (1 Chr 3:1–9) and insists this choice was not merely David’s fondness or a promise to Bathsheba, but God’s own will and appointment.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/28.htm
- **Constable** notes that this was a significant event because Israel had never had a hereditary monarchy before — Saul was not succeeded by any son.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-28.html

### v. 6 — God’s Promise to Solomon
God declared: Solomon shall build My house and courts, for I have chosen him as My son, and I will be his Father.

- **Gill** links this to 2 Samuel 7:13–14 and Ephesians 1:5 (predestined to adoption as sons). The phrase “I will be his Father” denotes special favor and covenant relationship.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/28.htm

### v. 7 — Conditional Establishment of the Kingdom
God will establish Solomon’s kingdom forever **if** he remains steadfast (or “constant,” KJV) in keeping God’s commandments.

- **Gill** notes that the “if” clause was not part of Nathan’s original oracle (since Solomon was not yet born) but was an added revelation given to David later, as the text implies.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/28.htm
- **Constable** observes that the plural imperatives in the Hebrew of vv. 7–9 show that David’s charge to remain faithful was directed to all the assembled leaders, not only to Solomon.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-28.html

### v. 8 — Charge to the Whole Assembly
In the sight of all Israel and in the hearing of God, the people are to “keep and seek out all the commandments of the LORD” so that they may possess the land and leave it as an inheritance forever.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)** unpacks the threefold exhortation: (1) be *careful* — regard obedience as important; (2) *seek out* — search the Scriptures diligently; (3) *all* the commandments — not just a few favorites.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-28/
- **Gill** says “keep and seek” means seek to know them, search for them in God’s word, and endeavour to keep them, quoting Isaiah 1:19 for the principle that by obedience they held the land.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/28.htm
- **The Pulpit Commentary** calls this double charge (first to the people, then to Solomon) “full of force and majesty” and notes the language echoes Deuteronomy 4:21, 26; 30:19.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-28.html

### v. 9 — David’s Personal Charge to Solomon
“Know the God of your father, and serve Him with a whole heart and a willing mind, for the LORD searches every heart and understands every intent of the thoughts. If you seek Him, He will be found by you; but if you forsake Him, He will reject you forever.”

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: The command to *know* comes before the command to *serve* — “all failure in service is the result of loss of vision of God” (Morgan). David also calls for both heart and mind, not one or the other. Both halves of verse 9 proved true in Solomon’s life: he sought God at Gibeon and found Him (1 Kgs 3); he forsook God and was cast off (1 Kgs 11).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-28/
- **Gill**: “Know” means practical, experiential knowledge — to own and acknowledge God, to love and fear Him. “A perfect heart” means serving cordially and sincerely, not hypocritically. The Lord “searches all hearts” — even kings — and knows the first motions of the mind before thoughts are fully formed (cf. Gen 6:5).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/28.htm
- **Spurgeon** preached an entire sermon (“Sincere Seekers Assured Finders,” Feb. 26, 1871) on verse 9. He applies it universally: “If thou seek him, he will be found of thee” applies to any unconverted person. The promise is straightforward — seek God through faith in Christ and you will find Him. There is not, and never will be, a soul in hell who can say “I sought mercy through Christ and did not find it.” He rejects the objection “I am too guilty,” “too good,” “too poor,” “too ignorant,” or “no time.” The “cannot” of spiritual inability is really a “will not.”
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/1-chronicles-28.html
- **The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics)** notes that “know the God of thy father” means a practical knowledge and fear of God, analogous to “hear” meaning practical obedience. The expression “the God of thy father” is intentionally touching, anticipating verse 20 (“God, even my God”).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-28.html
- **Garner‑Howes Baptist Commentary** (search excerpt) summarizes David’s instructions to Solomon under five points: (1) know the God of David savingly; (2) serve with a perfect, willing heart; (3) remember the Lord knows all human imperfections and will judge accordingly; (4) if Solomon seeks, God will be found (Isa 55:6); (5) if he forsakes, God will forsake him (1 Kgs 11:4).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-chronicles-28.html

### v. 10 — “Be Strong and Do It”
“Consider now that the LORD has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary. Be strong and do it.”

- **Gill** renders “take heed now” — beware of offending God by forsaking Him, and set about the work with vigor and resolution. The Targum reads: “the Word of the Lord hath chosen thee.”
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/28.htm
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)** says David concluded his exhortation with the single most urgent command — build the temple. All of David’s exhaustive preparations would be for nothing if Solomon did not complete the task.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-28/

### vv. 11–13 — David Delivers the Temple Plans
David gave Solomon the plans for the portico, the temple buildings, storehouses, upper rooms, inner rooms, the mercy‑seat chamber, the courts, the surrounding chambers, the treasuries, the divisions of priests and Levites, and every article of service.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: David did nearly everything except actually build — he gave Solomon security, location, land, money, materials, staff, workers, and now the plans. The plans came “by the Spirit” (v. 12), not human ingenuity. Spurgeon is quoted: “Moreover, the temple was for God’s own dwelling. Should not the Most High have a house after his own mind?”
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-28/
- **Gill**: The “pattern” encompassed the porch (east entrance), the holy place and most holy place, the side chambers (1 Kgs 6:5), the treasuries, upper chambers where priests met, inner parlours where they ate holy things, and the place of the mercy seat. All this was “by the Spirit” — the Holy Spirit revealed it, just as the tabernacle pattern was given to Moses.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/28.htm
- **Gaebelein** strongly argues that “by the Spirit” (v. 12) means the Holy Spirit, not David’s own mind. He criticizes commentators who say the patterns were merely “floating in his mind”; the text says the Holy Spirit revealed it by inspiration, as with Moses.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-chronicles-28.html
- **Pulpit Commentary**: Notes a scholarly debate — Bertheau, Keil, and others regard “the spirit” as David’s own mind. But the Pulpit Commentary rejects this, arguing that the stress on the patterns being God‑given and now transferable to Solomon makes a merely human interpretation inadmissible.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-28.html
- **Constable** notes that the Chronicler presents the temple as “the palace of the Great King” — not merely a religious center but the house of Yahweh, the Sovereign’s palace where vassals came to offer allegiance (citing Merrill).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-28.html

### vv. 14–18 — The Weight of Gold and Silver for Every Article
David specified by weight the gold and silver for every article: lampstands (gold and silver), tables of showbread, forks, sprinkling bowls, pitchers, dishes, bowls, the altar of incense (refined gold), and “the chariot — the gold cherubim that spread their wings and overshadowed the ark.”

- **Gill**: Each item had its weight divinely directed. The gold lampstands were ten, each with seven lamps (1 Kgs 7:49); the tables of showbread were ten (2 Chr 4:8). Each gold item weighed about 100 pounds. The silver tables were for flaying or slaying sacrifices (Ezek 40:39). The gold cherubim were two large ones (1 Kgs 6:23), making four with the Mosaic cherubim, forming the “chariot” — imagery alluded to in Ezekiel’s vision. The ark with cherubim weighed about 200 pounds of pure gold (Jacob Leon).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/28.htm
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Gold is mentioned 11 times in six verses. The “chariot” is so called because God sat between the cherubim (Ps 99:1) and rode upon them (Ps 18:10). Trapp adds a note: “by this chariot of the cherubims God gave his people to understand that his presence in the ark was not so fixed among them, but that [He] would leave them, and ride clean away from them, if they should thereunto provoke him by their sins.”
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-28/

### v. 19 — “The LORD Made Me Understand in Writing by His Hand Upon Me”
David declares that all the details of the plan were made clear to him by the LORD in writing, by His hand upon him.

- **Gill** considers two possibilities: (1) an inward impulse of the Spirit that impressed the plan on David’s mind as clearly as if written down; (2) an actual handwriting from the Lord through angelic mediation, as with Moses receiving the tablets. The Hebrew word order suggests “the whole of this in writing from the hand of the LORD, unto me, he made me to understand.”
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/28.htm
- **Constable**: God revealed the temple plans to David as specifically as He had revealed the tabernacle plans to Moses (Exodus 25–31). The post‑exilic Jews must have had more detailed plans than survive today.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-28.html
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The text says “the whole in writing from the hand of Jehovah upon me, he made me to understand — all the works of this pattern.” Whatever one believes about the “writing” of the tablets of the Law by the finger of God (Ex 24:12; 31:18), the Chronicler presents the temple plans as having the same Divine origin as the tabernacle.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-28.html

### vv. 20–21 — Final Charge: “Be Strong and Courageous”
David tells Solomon: “Be strong and courageous, and do it. Do not be afraid or discouraged, for the LORD God, my God, is with you. He will not fail you or forsake you until all the work is finished.” He then assures Solomon that the divisions of priests and Levites are ready, every willing, skillful worker is at his disposal, and the officials and people are fully at his command.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: David deliberately echoes God’s words to Joshua (Josh 1:5–7), presenting Solomon as a second Joshua who must finish what Moses (David) could only prepare. Spurgeon is quoted: “Do not talk about it; do not sit down, and dream over the plans, and think how admirable they are, and then roll them up; but, ‘Be strong and of good courage, and do it.’”
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-28/
- **Constable** likewise notes the Moses‑David / Joshua‑Solomon typology, citing Williamson and Dillard.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-28.html
- **Gill**: The promise “He will not fail thee nor forsake thee” is taken from Joshua 1:5 and is applicable to every believer in any good work. The Targum renders “the Word of the Lord God, my God, will be thy help.”
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/28.htm
- **Precept Austin** notes that David wanted “anyone in the land with any responsibility or influence” to hear his final appeals — what had been a personal ambition was now a national responsibility (Hay, *What the Bible Teaches*).
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-28-commentary

## Points of Difference Among Protestant Traditions

### Baptist View
- The **Garner‑Howes Baptist Commentary** emphasizes “saving knowledge” of God, a “willing heart,” and warns that forsaking God brings His forsaking (citing 1 Kings 11:4). It frames verse 9 in terms of personal salvation and the need for wholehearted service.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-chronicles-28.html
- **Spurgeon** (Baptist) applied verse 9 evangelistically, insisting that any sinner who seeks God through faith in Christ *will* be found. He stressed the simplicity of the gospel over against sacramental or priestly mediation (“without paraphernalia, or altar, or sacrifice of the Mass”).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/1-chronicles-28.html

### Pentecostal / Charismatic View
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)** emphasizes that the temple plans were given “by the Spirit” (vv. 12, 19) — the Holy Spirit directly inspiring practical details of worship, not human ingenuity. The application emphasizes relationship with God (“know the God of your father”) as foundational to all service. There is a strong emphasis on the heart–mind combination (v. 9): “Some people are all heart and no mind … others all mind and no heart. Both are needed.” The commentary also underscores that God’s purposes sometimes require seasons of warfare before seasons of peace.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-28/

### Reformed / Presbyterian
- No directly searched Reformed sources were retrievable within limits, but the **Pulpit Commentary** (often representing mainstream Protestant scholarship) and **Constable** intersect with Reformed covenant theology. Constable sees the Davidic Covenant as the heart of Chronicles, emphasizing God’s sovereign election of David’s line and the conditional/unconditional tension of verse 7. The “Moses–David / Joshua–Solomon” typology points forward to Christ as the faithful Son of David.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-28.html

### Lutheran, Methodist, Anglican
- No Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Wesleyan/Methodist (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), or distinctively Anglican sources were retrieved within the tool limits. *Not found in this search.*

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship / Critical Notes
- **Constable** (citing Williamson and Dillard) reports the scholarly view that the Chronicler deliberately shaped the narrative to present David as a second Moses and Solomon as a second Joshua — a literary and theological patterning.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-28.html
- A debate exists over whether “by the Spirit” (v. 12) refers to the Holy Spirit or David’s own mind. **Bertheau and Keil** (cited by the Pulpit Commentary) argued it meant “the pattern of all that floated before his mind.” The Pulpit Commentary rejects this as inadequate given the manifest stress on divine origin.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-28.html
- **NET Bible notes** and **Bible Odyssey** could not be fetched within limits. *Not found.*
